# APX Data Specification: Use Case Document

*Proposed additions to the APDS data model · Draft for the APDS committee · based on APDS 4.1 (2026-01-14) · APX 0.14.0*

## Introduction

This document gives worked examples of the proposed data elements in use.
It continues the APDS 4.1 Use Case Document: APDS clause C.1 holds the
domain examples and C.2 the additional use cases, so the APX examples are
numbered C.3. Several build directly on APDS examples, in particular
C.2.2 (parking enforcement and user check-in) and C.2.4 (a parking
discount scheme).

Each example describes an operation in plain terms, then explains how
the existing APDS data and the proposed additions together support it.
The examples describe data only. How the data is requested or delivered
between systems is outside their scope.

## C.3 APX use cases

### C.3.1 Lane equipment status at a city-centre garage

A 600-space garage has two entry and two exit lanes. Each lane has an LPR
camera, a barrier, an intercom and, at the entry lanes, a ticket
dispenser. The operator uses a remote monitoring centre to answer
intercom calls after hours, and the city's parking guidance system shows
the garage on its signs.

At 22:10 the barrier on exit lane 2 fails to close. A queue forms at
lane 1. The monitoring centre must see the fault, take calls from lane 1,
and the guidance system should stop sending vehicles while the exit is
congested.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Place.** The garage, its vehicular accesses and its lane equipment are
described once as a Place hierarchy. Each barrier, intercom and ticket
dispenser is a SupplementalEquipment with an equipment type from
EquipmentTypeEnum, using the new values barrier, intercom and
ticketDispenser, and each camera uses the existing value lprCamera. Each
VehicularAccess lists its LaneCameras with their facing.

**Equipment status.** When the barrier fails, the site system sends one
EquipmentStatus record: the barrier's reference, equipmentStatus
'faulted' and the statusChangeTime. The monitoring centre and the guidance
system receive the same record and understand it the same way. When the
barrier is repaired, a second record with 'available' closes the episode.
Neither party needs the Place hierarchy resent.

**Observation.** Plate reads from each lane carry the cameraID on their
images. Because each LaneCamera states which way it faces, a receiver can
tell entering from exiting vehicles without knowing the camera vendor's
own configuration.

### C.3.2 Showing the sign at appeal

A surface lot changes its maximum stay from 3 hours to 2 hours on
1 March. The entrance sign is replaced that morning. On 4 March a
customer receives a parking charge notice and appeals, saying the sign
allowed 3 hours.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Place and Signage.** The lot holds two Signage records for the
entrance. The first, effective from the previous year, says 3 hours and
is now 'superseded' with effectiveTo 1 March 08:00. The second says
2 hours, is 'active' and is effective from 1 March 08:00. Each has a
photo and a location.

**Enforcement.** The violation record refers to the Place and the time of
the event. The appeals body selects the Signage record in force at that
time and sees the wording and photo of the sign as it stood, which here
shows the 2-hour limit.

### C.3.3 Monthly occupancy report to a city

A city licenses private car parks and asks each operator for monthly
occupancy reports: for each car park, the highest and average occupancy
for each hour of each day.

An operator's garage records a DemandType reading every two minutes,
about 21,600 readings a month.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Place.** The garage is described as a Place with its Supply, as it is
today.

**Occupancy.** For each hour the operator sends one DemandType inside a
DemandTable for the garage. Each carries periodStart and periodEnd for
the hour, maximumCount and averageCount, and sampleCount (normally 30).
An hour in which the counting system was offline carries a sampleCount
of 0 and no counts, so the city can see the gap rather than mistake it
for an empty garage. The month is about 720 records instead of 21,600,
and every operator in the city reports in the same form.

### C.3.4 Negotiated rate offered by a customer-service agent

A city-centre garage publishes its rate deck to a remote customer-service
provider and to an event-ticketing partner. Besides the hourly RateTables,
the deck contains a "Lost ticket, flat" table and an "Event organiser,
flat" table. The operator wants agents to be able to offer the lost-ticket
rate to a caller at the exit, and the partner to sell the event rate, but
nobody to offer the hourly early-bird table outside its hours.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Rates.** The operator sets `negotiable` to TRUE on the two flat tables
and gives each a `negotiatedRateLabel` ("Lost ticket – flat 20.00").
Every party mirroring the rate deck receives the flag with the table, so
the agent's screen and the partner's catalogue list only cleared tables,
and both show the operator's own wording.

**Session and Right.** When the agent applies the lost-ticket rate to the
vehicle in the lane, the Segment of the Session references the chosen
RateTable as it does today, and the resulting Payment can name the rate
sold (see the Right additions), so revenue reports show which negotiated
rate was used.

### C.3.5 First two hours free at a cinema

A cinema validates parking at the shopping-centre car park: the first two
hours are free for its customers.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Rates.** The cinema's ValidationProgram carries a ValidationBenefit with
`discountDuration` of two hours and the description "First 2 hours free".
A pay station can show the description to the customer before applying it.

**Session.** When the ticket is validated, the redemption records the
amount actually removed (for a three-hour stay, the price of the first two
hours at the applicable RateTable), and the Segment carries the validation
reference as APDS 4.1 already provides.

### C.3.6 Lost keycard at a monthly-parker garage

A tenant of an office building parks with an RFID keycard under a
monthly AssignedRight. On Tuesday the tenant reports the card lost. The
operator's office issues a replacement card with a new number and charges
a new deposit. The garage's lane controllers come from one vendor, and the
building's enforcement patrol uses a different vendor's handheld.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Right.** The original CredentialAssigned moves to `credentialStatus`
lost. The replacement is a new CredentialAssigned on the same
AssignedRight, `credentialStatus` active, with `replacesCredentialId`
pointing to the old card; the old card gains `replacedByCredentialId` and
moves to replaced. The replacement's CredentialMedia records the medium
(physicalCard), the stock serial number and the deposit, with
`depositStatus` held. Both vendors read the same AssignedRight, so the
lane refuses the old card and the handheld treats the old number as
replaced at the same moment.

**Session.** If someone presents the old card at the entry lane, the
access event proposed in the Session additions records a denial with the
reason "credential replaced". Because the card is still on file, the event
references the credential; a card that matched nothing would instead be
recorded as a PresentedCredential.

### C.3.7 Multi-vehicle residential permit with a renewal

A city issues annual residential permits. A household registers three
vehicles under one permit but only two may be parked in the zone at once;
a third is charged the day rate. In December the household renews for the
following year.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Right.** The permit is an AssignedRight with three VehicleCredentials,
as in the APDS annual-permit use case. It carries
`maxConcurrentVehicles` 2 and an OverageBilling with mode dayRate and the
day-rate amount. The renewal is a new AssignedRight whose
`renewsAssignedRightId` references the current permit; the current permit
gains `renewedByAssignedRightId`, so the city's portal and the
enforcement vendor can follow the chain.

**Session and Observation.** When an enforcement vehicle reads a third
registered plate while two Sessions are already open under the permit,
the enforcement system finds the overage from the permit itself and bills
the day rate, without a separate agreement with the permit vendor.

**Right (plate lists).** The city also shares a scofflaw PlateList with
the car parks in the zone. PlateListPlaceFlags set `alertOnArrival` at
every car park and `refuseService` at the city-owned ones only. A car park
that only screens arrivals holds a CredentialDigest per entry instead of
the plates themselves.

### C.3.8 Gated garage with plate recognition at entry and exit

City Centre Garage has two entry lanes and two exit lanes, each with a
plate recognition camera and a barrier. Monthly parkers hold a keycard;
transient customers are identified by their plate. A third-party
analytics provider receives the garage's Sessions to report occupancy and
average dwell to the city.

On Monday morning a monthly parker presents a keycard that was reported
lost on Friday and replaced. The reader refuses it. Later a transient
vehicle leaves through an exit lane, but its entry was not recorded
because the entry camera was being cleaned. On Wednesday a vehicle that
entered on Saturday has still not been seen leaving.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Access events.** The refusal is recorded as an `AccessEvent` with
`direction` entry, `outcome` denied and `denialReason`
`credentialReplaced`, referencing the old `CredentialAssigned` and the
reader as `SupplementalEquipment`. The help desk that answers the
intercom, the card issuer and the operator all see the same record,
although no Session was opened.

**Sessions.** The transient exit produces a Session whose
`SessionClosure` has `endReason` `exitOnly` and `startObserved` false; its
start time is a placeholder. The analytics provider leaves it out of
dwell statistics and occupancy instead of counting a visit of zero
minutes. The Saturday vehicle's Session is closed by the operator's rule
with `endReason` `stale`, `endInferred` true and `closureRule` naming the
rule, so it is not mistaken for an observed exit.

**Observations.** Each Session lists its `SessionRead` entries: the entry
and exit observations, and any duplicate frames from a second camera
marked `duplicate`, so a receiver never counts one passage twice.

### C.3.9 Merchant validation at a shopping centre

A cinema validates parking for its customers through a pay station code
and through its own application. The car park operator invoices the
cinema monthly.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Validation redemption.** Each validation applied is a
`ValidationRedemption` referencing the cinema's validation program, the
Session, the time, the channel (`payStation` or `merchantApp`) and the
amount actually removed. A customer who stayed 20 minutes and was charged
nothing records the 20 minutes' fee, not the nominal three hours.

**Sessions.** The redemption's `validationId` is written to the Segment's
existing `validationId`, so a receiver that knows only APDS 4.1 still sees
that the Segment was validated.

**Corrections.** A redemption applied in error is not deleted; its
`redemptionStatus` becomes `reversed` with the time and reason, so the
monthly invoice and the audit trail agree.

### C.3.10 Gateless car park with plate recognition and review

A supermarket car park has no barriers. One camera faces the shared
entrance and exit. Customers may stay 90 minutes free; longer stays
receive a parking charge notice, and the national code of practice
requires a person to confirm each plate first.

A vehicle arrives at 10:02 and leaves at 12:10. Its exit read reports
plate `AB12 CDE` with plate confidence 0.97, but colour confidence only
0.41 because of glare.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Observations.** Each read carries an `AttributeRead` for the plate, the
country, the make and the colour, each with its own confidence, and
`movement` toward or away from the camera. Because the entrance and exit
share one camera, the movement is what tells the two passages apart; the
recognition system reports `accessDirection` entry or exit accordingly.
Several frames of each passage share one `captureGroup` and are treated
as one event.

**Review.** Because a charge notice will follow, the exit read is sent to
review with `reviewReason` `enforcementHandoff`. The reviewer sees the
`AlternateRead` candidates (`AB12 CDF`, 0.62) and confirms the original.
The read's `ReadReview` records `confirmed`, the time and the reviewer,
and travels with the observation to the enforcement system.

**Sessions.** The Session built from the two reads lists them as its
entry and exit (`SessionRead`), so the 128-minute stay can be checked
against the observations it rests on.

### C.3.11 Valet drop-off and a damage claim

A hotel valet takes a guest's car at 18:30. The attendant photographs the
car and notes a scuff on the rear bumper. At handback the next morning
the guest reports a dent on the driver's door.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Condition reports.** The drop-off `ConditionReport` holds the
photographs, a `DamageItem` for the rear bumper with severity `minor`,
and the guest's acknowledgement. The handback report adds a `DamageItem`
for the driver's door. Comparing the two reports, item by item, is the
evidence the claim is answered with.

**Sessions.** The valet ticket (Session domain) references both reports,
the APDS Session for the stay and the Space where the car was parked, so
the operator can see who parked it, where, and when.

### C.3.12 Charging inside a parking stay at a controlled garage

A city-centre garage has twelve charging points on level 2, each over a
marked bay with an overhead camera. Drivers enter through LPR-equipped
lanes. A driver arrives, parks in bay 2-07 and plugs in. The charge is
authorized by the plate read at entry. After 90 minutes the vehicle is
full, but the driver returns two hours later. The garage applies a
10-minute grace period and then an idle fee, and the charge is paid
together with the parking at exit.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Place.** The charging points are already described in APDS as
SupplementalEquipment with ElectricChargingPoints and Connectors, and each
bay is a Space. Nothing new is needed to describe what is installed.

**Energy Infrastructure.** A ChargingPointStatus for bay 2-07 moves from
`available` to `charging`, then to `occupied` once delivery ends with the
cable still connected, using the existing `RefillPointStatusEnum`. Its
ChargingBayPresence reads `vehiclePluggedIn` from the overhead camera. A
ChargingSession records the authorization, the plug-in, the start and end
of charging, the start of idle time after the grace period, and the
unplug. It records the energy delivered, the idle terms in force when the
charge began, and a ChargingCost with energy and idle components. Its
settlement mode is `parkingSession`.

**Session.** The ChargingSession references the driver's APDS Session.
At exit, the parking system adds the charging cost to the stay and takes
one Payment for both.

**Observation.** The entry plate read and the camera evidence for the bay
are APDS Observations. The bay presence references the camera
Observation, and the charging session references the credential observed
at entry.

### C.3.13 A bay taken by a vehicle that is not charging

At the same garage, a vehicle parks in bay 2-09 and does not plug in. The
camera sees a vehicle, while the charger reports no cable connected. After
the place's grace period the operator wants an attendant to act.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Energy Infrastructure.** The ChargingBayPresence for bay 2-09 reads
`vehicleNotPluggedIn` from the overhead camera, with `evCapable` false
where the camera recognizes the vehicle model. The ChargingPointStatus is
`blocked`.

**Operations.** An Alert of type `evBayNotCharging` (or `iceInEvSpace`) is
raised for the bay's SupplementalEquipment and references the camera
Observation as evidence.

**Enforcement.** Where the place's EnforcementPolicy allows it, the
condition can become a Violation of type `restrictedSpace`, with the camera
Image as evidence.

### C.3.14 Records arriving through a regional hub

A regional parking hub collects Place and Session data from 40 operators
and passes it to the city. One operator also sends its Place data to the
city directly. The city therefore receives some Place records twice:
once from the operator and once from the hub.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**PkCommon.** Records the hub forwards keep their identification and
carry RecordType.origin naming the operator system that created them.
Records the operator sends directly carry no origin, because the operator
created them. The city sees that both copies come from the same source
and keeps one. When a record is wrong, the city knows to raise it with
the operator rather than with the hub.

**Place and Session.** Nothing else changes. Places and Sessions are
exchanged exactly as today, which is in line with the Overview's
guidance that a Receiving Party should confirm data ownership when the
same record arrives from different Distributing Parties.

### C.3.15 C.2.2 continued: from transaction exception to notice and appeal

This example continues Use Case C.2.2. At Hangzhou Xiaoshan International
Airport, garage P6 logs entry and exit by licence plate camera, and
customers check in to their space by app. The use case lists transaction
exceptions, such as a vehicle checked in to a reserved space without a
valid reservation or an ICE vehicle in an EV space. It notes that these
"can be converted into violation notices that create fines/penalties for
the owner of the vehicle", that an enforcement officer cannot cancel
violations generated by the system, and that an officer can create new
violations from their own observations.

The airport uses a processing agency to send notices and collect payment,
and an independent adjudicator to hear appeals. Here is what happens next.

1. At 14:05 a vehicle checks in by app to reserved space P6-B-112 with no
   AssignedRight for that space. The grace period passes, and the system
   records a Violation with status `detected`.
2. An officer on patrol finds a second vehicle in an EV space with no
   charging connection and records a Violation on their handheld.
3. A reviewer confirms the first violation. A notice is posted to the
   registered keeper, and the keeper pays.
4. The keeper of the second vehicle appeals, saying the signs were unclear.
   The adjudicator reduces the amount.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Observation.** The entry read, the check-in and the patrol officer's
photographs are APDS Observations and Images, exactly as C.2.2 describes.
Each Violation references the Observations it was built from and carries
the photographs as evidence Images with their Location.

**Session and Right.** The first Violation references the vehicle's Session
and, as its related AssignedRight, the reservation held for a different
space. Its type is `wrongPlace`. The second has no covering right, and its
type is `restrictedSpace`.

**Enforcement.** The first Violation has detection mode `automated`. Because
the garage's EnforcementPolicy does not allow unreviewed issuance, it moves
from `detected` to `confirmed` only after review, then to `issued`. Its
Notice carries the notice number, the time of issue, kind
`penaltyChargeNotice` and delivery method `post`. The policy's
NoticeDeliveryRule allows posting for automated findings only within 14
days of the observation and with at least two Images, and the processing
agency can check both before sending. When the keeper pays, the Payment is
referenced and the status becomes `paid`, then `closed`.

The second Violation has detection mode `manual` and references the
officer's Contact. Matching C.2.2, the officer can create this violation but
not cancel the system's. Its Notice is `affixedToVehicle`. The keeper opens
an Appeal with reason `signageInadequate`. The adjudicator compares the
Violation with the Signage in force at the space when it was observed, then
records resolution `reduced` with an adjusted amount. The violation returns
to `issued` at the lower amount.

**Place.** Both violations reference the same Place elements, Spaces and
SupplementalEquipment (cameras and handheld devices) that the rest of the
model describes. The EnforcementPolicy applies to the whole of P6 through
the Place hierarchy.

### C.3.16 Escalation of an unpaid notice on street

A city issues a penalty charge notice for an on-street overstay. Its
EnforcementPolicy sets a payment grace period of 14 days, an EscalationStep
adding 50% after 28 days, and a PenaltyLimit capping the total at twice the
amount at issue.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Enforcement.** The Violation's amount rises once, after 28 days without
payment, and never above the PenaltyLimit. Any party holding the
EnforcementPolicy version referenced by the Violation can confirm the
increase was lawful. Time spent under appeal does not count towards the
step.

**Right.** The overstay is found against an AssignedRight whose validity
had ended. That right is referenced as the related AssignedRight, with
type `expiredRight`.

### C.3.17 A barrier fault seen by every party that needs it

A shopping-centre car park has its barriers and pay stations maintained by
the equipment supplier, is watched overnight by a remote monitoring
centre, and is run by an operator. At 22:40 the exit barrier on lane 3
stops responding, and a vehicle is waiting.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Place.** The lane is a VehicularAccess element and the barrier is
SupplementalEquipment in the Place hierarchy. Its status changes to
`fault` through the device status proposed in the Place domain.

**Operations.** The lane controller raises an Alert of type `deviceFault`,
severity `major`, referencing the barrier and the lane. A second Alert of
type `laneBlocked` follows when the waiting vehicle is detected. The
monitoring centre acknowledges both, so the operator's duty manager can see
they are being handled. When the supplier's engineer repairs the barrier,
both alerts are resolved. All three parties work from the same records,
with the time each condition began, when it was detected, and when it was
dealt with.

**Observation.** The waiting vehicle's plate read is an APDS Observation.
The `laneBlocked` alert references it as the related record.

### C.3.18 C.2.2 transaction exceptions as alerts

At Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport (Use Case C.2.2), the system
detects a vehicle occupying space P6-B-112 without a check-in, and another
that checked out but has not exited within the grace period.

These specifications support this use case in a number of ways:

**Operations.** Each exception becomes an Alert, of type
`occupiedWithoutCheckIn` and `noCheckOut` respectively, referencing the
space and the related Session. The enforcement officers' devices show the
open alerts.

**Enforcement.** An officer who confirms that an exception is a violation
creates a Violation that references the same Session and Observations
(see the Enforcement domain). The Alert is then resolved.

## Annex D (informative) Example external code lists

APDS Annex D gives example user-defined code lists. APX publishes the
following lists in the same `UserDefinedCodeList` shape. They show how
deployments would extend the enumerations proposed in this document, and
they seeded the proposed values.

| APX code list | Extends |
| --- | --- |
| `apx-access-denial-reasons` | Access denial reasons on an access event |
| `apx-device-states` | Equipment status |
| `apx-session-end-reasons` | Session end reasons |
| `apx-read-review-reasons` | Reasons a plate read was sent for review |
| `apx-violation-types` | Violation types |
| `apx-plate-list-categories` | Plate list categories |
| `apx-payment-line-codes` | Payment line codes |
| `apx-alert-types` | Alert types |
| `apx-issue-types` | Customer service issue types |
| `apx-toll-dispute-reasons`, `apx-toll-dispute-resolutions` | Toll dispute reasons and resolutions |

The lists are published at <https://github.com/rneubauer/apx/tree/main/spec/registries>.
